<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
<meta charset="UTF-8" />
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0" />
<title>E-Portfolio · DPE 104 · Carlo Gonzaga</title>
<link href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Cormorant+Garamond:ital,wght@0,300;0,400;0,600;0,700;1,300;1,400;1,600&family=DM+Sans:wght@300;400;500;600&family=Playfair+Display:ital,wght@0,700;1,400&display=swap" rel="stylesheet" />
<style>
  :root {
    --navy: #0f1f3d;
    --gold: #c9a84c;
    --gold-light: #e8d5a3;
    --cream: #faf7f2;
    --warm-white: #fffef9;
    --muted: #7a7060;
    --text: #1a1510;
    --soft: #e8e4dc;
    --accent: #2a4a7f;
  }

  * { margin: 0; padding: 0; box-sizing: border-box; }

  body {
    font-family: 'DM Sans', sans-serif;
    background: var(--cream);
    color: var(--text);
    overflow-x: hidden;
  }

  /* COVER GATE */
  #cover {
    position: fixed;
    inset: 0;
    z-index: 1000;
    display: flex;
    flex-direction: column;
    align-items: center;
    justify-content: center;
    background: var(--navy);
    text-align: center;
    padding: 2rem;
    transition: opacity 0.8s ease, transform 0.8s ease;
  }
  #cover.hidden {
    opacity: 0;
    transform: translateY(-30px);
    pointer-events: none;
  }
  .cover-badge {
    font-size: 0.72rem;
    letter-spacing: 0.22em;
    text-transform: uppercase;
    color: var(--gold);
    margin-bottom: 2.5rem;
    opacity: 0;
    animation: fadeUp 0.9s 0.3s forwards;
  }
  .cover-title {
    font-family: 'Cormorant Garamond', serif;
    font-size: clamp(2.6rem, 7vw, 5rem);
    font-weight: 300;
    color: var(--warm-white);
    line-height: 1.08;
    margin-bottom: 0.4rem;
    opacity: 0;
    animation: fadeUp 0.9s 0.5s forwards;
  }
  .cover-title strong {
    font-weight: 700;
    font-style: italic;
    color: var(--gold-light);
  }
  .cover-divider {
    width: 60px;
    height: 1px;
    background: var(--gold);
    margin: 1.8rem auto;
    opacity: 0;
    animation: fadeUp 0.9s 0.7s forwards;
  }
  .cover-sub {
    font-family: 'Cormorant Garamond', serif;
    font-size: 1.15rem;
    font-style: italic;
    color: rgba(255,255,255,0.5);
    margin-bottom: 0.5rem;
    opacity: 0;
    animation: fadeUp 0.9s 0.9s forwards;
  }
  .cover-name {
    font-family: 'Cormorant Garamond', serif;
    font-size: 1.5rem;
    font-weight: 600;
    color: var(--gold-light);
    letter-spacing: 0.03em;
    opacity: 0;
    animation: fadeUp 0.9s 1.1s forwards;
  }
  .cover-quote {
    max-width: 520px;
    font-size: 0.82rem;
    font-style: italic;
    color: rgba(255,255,255,0.28);
    line-height: 1.75;
    margin: 2.5rem auto;
    opacity: 0;
    animation: fadeUp 0.9s 1.3s forwards;
  }
  .open-btn {
    display: inline-flex;
    align-items: center;
    gap: 0.75rem;
    background: transparent;
    border: 1.5px solid var(--gold);
    color: var(--gold);
    font-family: 'DM Sans', sans-serif;
    font-size: 0.82rem;
    font-weight: 500;
    letter-spacing: 0.15em;
    text-transform: uppercase;
    padding: 1rem 2.4rem;
    cursor: pointer;
    transition: all 0.35s ease;
    opacity: 0;
    animation: fadeUp 0.9s 1.5s forwards;
    position: relative;
    overflow: hidden;
  }
  .open-btn::before {
    content: '';
    position: absolute;
    inset: 0;
    background: var(--gold);
    transform: translateX(-100%);
    transition: transform 0.35s ease;
    z-index: -1;
  }
  .open-btn:hover { color: var(--navy); }
  .open-btn:hover::before { transform: translateX(0); }
  .open-btn svg { transition: transform 0.3s ease; }
  .open-btn:hover svg { transform: translateX(4px); }
  .cover-footer {
    position: absolute;
    bottom: 2rem;
    font-size: 0.7rem;
    letter-spacing: 0.12em;
    color: rgba(255,255,255,0.18);
    text-transform: uppercase;
    opacity: 0;
    animation: fadeUp 0.9s 1.7s forwards;
  }

  /* MAIN */
  #portfolio { display: none; min-height: 100vh; }
  #portfolio.visible { display: block; }

  /* NAV */
  nav {
    position: sticky;
    top: 0;
    z-index: 100;
    background: var(--navy);
    padding: 0 3rem;
    display: flex;
    align-items: center;
    justify-content: space-between;
    height: 58px;
    box-shadow: 0 2px 20px rgba(0,0,0,0.18);
  }
  .nav-brand {
    font-family: 'Cormorant Garamond', serif;
    font-size: 1rem;
    font-weight: 600;
    color: var(--gold-light);
  }
  .nav-links { display: flex; gap: 0.2rem; list-style: none; }
  .nav-links a {
    display: flex;
    align-items: center;
    gap: 0.4rem;
    padding: 0.4rem 0.85rem;
    font-size: 0.72rem;
    font-weight: 500;
    letter-spacing: 0.1em;
    text-transform: uppercase;
    color: rgba(255,255,255,0.5);
    text-decoration: none;
    transition: color 0.2s;
  }
  .nav-links a:hover, .nav-links a.active { color: var(--gold); }
  .nav-num { font-family: 'Cormorant Garamond', serif; font-size: 0.9rem; font-style: italic; opacity: 0.5; }

  /* HERO */
  #hero {
    background: var(--navy);
    padding: 7rem 3rem 5rem;
    text-align: center;
    position: relative;
    overflow: hidden;
  }
  #hero::before {
    content: '';
    position: absolute;
    top: -40%; left: 50%;
    transform: translateX(-50%);
    width: 600px; height: 600px;
    border-radius: 50%;
    background: radial-gradient(circle, rgba(201,168,76,0.08) 0%, transparent 70%);
    pointer-events: none;
  }
  .hero-kicker { font-size: 0.72rem; letter-spacing: 0.22em; text-transform: uppercase; color: var(--gold); margin-bottom: 1.5rem; }
  .hero-title { font-family: 'Cormorant Garamond', serif; font-size: clamp(2.2rem, 5vw, 3.8rem); font-weight: 300; color: var(--warm-white); line-height: 1.1; margin-bottom: 0.3rem; }
  .hero-title em { font-style: italic; color: var(--gold-light); }
  .hero-divider { width: 48px; height: 1px; background: var(--gold); margin: 2rem auto; }
  .hero-author { font-family: 'Cormorant Garamond', serif; font-size: 1.4rem; color: white; }
  .hero-meta { font-size: 0.78rem; color: rgba(255,255,255,0.4); letter-spacing: 0.1em; margin-top: 0.4rem; }
  .hero-quote { max-width: 560px; margin: 3rem auto 0; font-family: 'Cormorant Garamond', serif; font-size: 1.05rem; font-style: italic; color: rgba(255,255,255,0.35); line-height: 1.8; }

  /* TOC */
  #toc { background: var(--warm-white); padding: 5rem 2.5rem; border-bottom: 1px solid var(--soft); }
  .toc-label { font-size: 0.68rem; letter-spacing: 0.22em; text-transform: uppercase; color: var(--gold); margin-bottom: 0.5rem; }
  .toc-heading { font-family: 'Cormorant Garamond', serif; font-size: 2rem; font-weight: 300; color: var(--navy); margin-bottom: 3rem; }
  .toc-grid { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr); gap: 1.5rem; max-width: 1100px; }
  .toc-card {
    border: 1px solid var(--soft);
    padding: 1.8rem;
    text-decoration: none;
    color: inherit;
    transition: all 0.3s ease;
    display: block;
    position: relative;
    overflow: hidden;
  }
  .toc-card::after { content: ''; position: absolute; bottom: 0; left: 0; right: 0; height: 2px; background: var(--gold); transform: scaleX(0); transform-origin: left; transition: transform 0.3s ease; }
  .toc-card:hover { border-color: var(--gold-light); box-shadow: 0 8px 30px rgba(0,0,0,0.06); transform: translateY(-2px); }
  .toc-card:hover::after { transform: scaleX(1); }
  .toc-num { font-family: 'Cormorant Garamond', serif; font-size: 2.8rem; font-weight: 700; color: var(--soft); line-height: 1; margin-bottom: 0.6rem; }
  .toc-title { font-family: 'Cormorant Garamond', serif; font-size: 1.1rem; font-weight: 700; color: var(--navy); margin-bottom: 0.4rem; }
  .toc-desc { font-size: 0.75rem; color: var(--muted); line-height: 1.5; }

  /* SECTION BAND */
  .band { background: var(--navy); padding: 3rem 2.5rem; display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 2rem; border-top: 3px solid var(--gold); }
  .band-num { font-family: 'Cormorant Garamond', serif; font-size: 5rem; font-weight: 700; color: rgba(255,255,255,0.07); line-height: 1; }
  .band-label { font-size: 0.68rem; letter-spacing: 0.2em; text-transform: uppercase; color: var(--gold); margin-bottom: 0.2rem; }
  .band-title { font-family: 'Cormorant Garamond', serif; font-size: 1.8rem; font-weight: 600; color: var(--warm-white); line-height: 1.15; }

  /* SECTION WRAP */
  .section-wrap { max-width: 860px; margin: 0 auto; padding: 5rem 2.5rem; }

  /* TYPOGRAPHY */
  .prose p { font-size: 0.98rem; line-height: 1.85; color: #2d2820; margin-bottom: 1.3rem; }
  .prose p:last-child { margin-bottom: 0; }

  /* GOALS */
  .goals-heading { font-family: 'Cormorant Garamond', serif; font-size: 1.3rem; font-weight: 700; color: var(--navy); margin: 2.5rem 0 1rem; }
  .goals-list { list-style: none; display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 0.85rem; }
  .goals-list li { display: flex; align-items: flex-start; gap: 1rem; font-size: 0.93rem; line-height: 1.65; color: #2d2820; }
  .goal-dot { flex-shrink: 0; width: 8px; height: 8px; border-radius: 50%; background: var(--gold); margin-top: 0.5rem; }

  /* TOPIC TAG */
  .topic-tag { display: inline-flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.6rem; background: var(--navy); color: var(--gold-light); font-size: 0.75rem; font-weight: 600; letter-spacing: 0.12em; text-transform: uppercase; padding: 0.5rem 1rem; margin-bottom: 2.5rem; }

  /* ARTIFACT HEADER */
  .artifact-header { display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 1.2rem; margin-bottom: 2rem; }
  .artifact-num-badge { background: var(--navy); color: var(--gold); font-size: 0.68rem; font-weight: 700; letter-spacing: 0.18em; text-transform: uppercase; padding: 0.45rem 1rem; white-space: nowrap; flex-shrink: 0; }
  .artifact-topic-title { font-family: 'Cormorant Garamond', serif; font-size: 1.5rem; font-weight: 700; color: var(--navy); line-height: 1.2; }
  .artifact-divider { width: 100%; height: 2px; background: linear-gradient(to right, var(--gold), transparent); margin: 3.5rem 0; }
  .table-label { font-size: 0.75rem; font-weight: 600; letter-spacing: 0.12em; text-transform: uppercase; color: var(--navy); margin: 1.5rem 0 0.75rem; }

  /* SUB-HEADING */
  .sub-heading { font-family: 'Cormorant Garamond', serif; font-size: 1.3rem; font-weight: 700; color: var(--navy); margin: 2.5rem 0 1rem; display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.7rem; }
  .sub-heading::after { content: ''; flex: 1; height: 1px; background: var(--soft); }

  /* COMPARE GRID */
  .compare-grid { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; gap: 1.5rem; margin: 2rem 0; }
  .compare-card { background: var(--cream); border: 1px solid var(--soft); padding: 1.8rem; }
  .compare-card-title { font-family: 'Cormorant Garamond', serif; font-size: 1rem; font-weight: 700; letter-spacing: 0.08em; color: var(--navy); text-transform: uppercase; margin-bottom: 1.2rem; padding-bottom: 0.7rem; border-bottom: 2px solid var(--gold); }
  .compare-row { font-size: 0.83rem; line-height: 1.6; color: #3a3228; margin-bottom: 0.65rem; }
  .compare-row strong { color: var(--navy); font-weight: 600; display: block; font-size: 0.73rem; text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: 0.06em; margin-bottom: 0.1rem; }

  /* TABLE */
  .styled-table { width: 100%; border-collapse: collapse; margin: 1.5rem 0; font-size: 0.82rem; }
  .styled-table th { background: var(--navy); color: var(--gold-light); padding: 0.8rem 1rem; text-align: left; font-weight: 600; letter-spacing: 0.06em; font-size: 0.73rem; text-transform: uppercase; }
  .styled-table td { padding: 0.85rem 1rem; border-bottom: 1px solid var(--soft); color: #2d2820; line-height: 1.55; vertical-align: top; }
  .styled-table tr:nth-child(even) td { background: rgba(201,168,76,0.04); }
  .styled-table td:first-child { font-weight: 600; color: var(--navy); }

  /* STRATEGIES */
  .strategies-grid { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(255px, 1fr)); gap: 1.2rem; margin: 2rem 0; }
  .strategy-card { background: var(--cream); border: 1px solid var(--soft); padding: 1.4rem; transition: box-shadow 0.25s, transform 0.25s; }
  .strategy-card:hover { box-shadow: 0 8px 25px rgba(0,0,0,0.07); transform: translateY(-2px); }
  .strat-num { font-family: 'Cormorant Garamond', serif; font-size: 1.8rem; font-weight: 700; color: var(--gold-light); line-height: 1; margin-bottom: 0.4rem; }
  .strat-name { font-weight: 600; font-size: 0.85rem; color: var(--navy); margin-bottom: 0.5rem; text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: 0.05em; }
  .strat-desc { font-size: 0.8rem; line-height: 1.6; color: var(--muted); }

  /* ARTIFACT BOX */
  .artifact-box { background: var(--navy); color: rgba(255,255,255,0.82); padding: 2rem 2.2rem; margin: 2rem 0; border-left: 4px solid var(--gold); }
  .artifact-label { font-size: 0.68rem; letter-spacing: 0.18em; text-transform: uppercase; color: var(--gold); margin-bottom: 0.5rem; }
  .artifact-box p { font-size: 0.88rem; line-height: 1.75; }

  /* REFLECTION */
  .reflection-block { background: rgba(201,168,76,0.05); border-left: 3px solid var(--gold); padding: 1.5rem 1.8rem; margin: 1.5rem 0; }
  .reflection-label { font-size: 0.68rem; letter-spacing: 0.18em; text-transform: uppercase; color: var(--gold); font-weight: 600; margin-bottom: 0.8rem; }
  .reflection-block p { font-size: 0.88rem; line-height: 1.8; font-style: italic; color: #3a3228; margin-bottom: 0.8rem; }
  .reflection-block p:last-child { margin-bottom: 0; }

  /* MASTERY */
  .mastery-box { background: var(--navy); padding: 2rem 2.2rem; margin: 2rem 0; }
  .mastery-label { font-size: 0.68rem; letter-spacing: 0.18em; text-transform: uppercase; color: var(--gold); margin-bottom: 0.8rem; }
  .mastery-box p { font-size: 0.88rem; line-height: 1.75; font-style: italic; color: rgba(255,255,255,0.78); }

  /* PHILOSOPHY QUOTE */
  .philosophy-quote { font-family: 'Cormorant Garamond', serif; font-size: 1.3rem; font-style: italic; font-weight: 400; color: var(--navy); text-align: center; line-height: 1.75; margin: 2.5rem auto; max-width: 560px; padding: 2rem; border-top: 1px solid var(--soft); border-bottom: 1px solid var(--soft); }

  /* ARTIFACT IMAGE */
  .artifact-image-wrap { margin: 1.5rem 0 2rem; border: 1px solid var(--soft); padding: 1.2rem; background: var(--cream); text-align: center; }
  .artifact-img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; display: block; margin: 0 auto; }
  .artifact-img-caption { font-size: 0.72rem; letter-spacing: 0.1em; text-transform: uppercase; color: var(--muted); margin-top: 0.8rem; }

  /* REFERENCES */
  .ref-list { display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 0.9rem; margin: 1.5rem 0 2.5rem; }
  .ref-item { font-size: 0.85rem; line-height: 1.7; color: #3a3228; padding-left: 1.5rem; border-left: 2px solid var(--soft); }
  .ref-item a { color: var(--accent); text-decoration: none; }
  .ref-item a:hover { text-decoration: underline; }
  .ack-block { background: var(--cream); border: 1px solid var(--soft); padding: 2rem 2.2rem; margin-top: 1.5rem; }
  .ack-block p { font-size: 0.88rem; line-height: 1.85; color: #3a3228; margin-bottom: 1rem; }
  .ack-block p:last-child { margin-bottom: 0; }

  /* FOOTER */
  footer { background: var(--navy); padding: 3rem; text-align: center; color: rgba(255,255,255,0.3); font-size: 0.75rem; letter-spacing: 0.08em; border-top: 1px solid rgba(201,168,76,0.2); }
  .f-logo { font-family: 'Cormorant Garamond', serif; font-size: 1.1rem; color: var(--gold-light); margin-bottom: 0.5rem; }

  @keyframes fadeUp {
    from { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(16px); }
    to { opacity: 1; transform: translateY(0); }
  }

  @media (max-width: 680px) {
    nav { padding: 0 1.2rem; }
    .nav-links a span:not(.nav-num) { display: none; }
    .section-wrap { padding: 3rem 1.2rem; }
    .compare-grid { grid-template-columns: 1fr; }
    .band { padding: 2rem 1.2rem; }
  }
</style>
</head>

  <!-- SECTION 01 -->
  <div id="s01">
    <div class="band">
      <div class="band-num">01</div>
      <div class="band-body">
        <p class="band-label">Section One</p>
        <h2 class="band-title">Introduction &amp; Learning Goals</h2>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div style="background:var(--cream)">
      <div class="section-wrap">
        <div class="prose">
          <p>My name is Carlo Gonzaga, and I came to this course carrying both a diploma and a dream that stretches far beyond myself. I graduated with a Bachelor of Science in Information and Communications Technology, earning the distinction of Cum Laude — a milestone I did not reach alone. Behind every late night and every studied page stood the quiet hopes of family members who once dreamed of walking this same path toward education. That inheritance of aspiration is what drives me. Every effort I invest in becoming an educator is not merely personal — it is a fulfillment of something larger; a promise kept across generations.</p>
          <p>As I entered this course, I carried with me the assumption that assessment was straightforward: a tool for measuring, grading, and concluding. What I did not anticipate was how profoundly the experience would reshape my entire understanding of that word. Through readings, discussions, and hands-on tasks, I came to see assessment not as a final verdict, but as an ongoing conversation between teacher and learner — a living process that informs, guides, and empowers rather than simply judges.</p>
          <p>I believe assessment matters in education because, at its core, it is an act of care. When done with intention and honesty, it tells students not only where they stand, but where they are capable of going. It gives teachers the evidence they need to reflect on and refine their practice. And perhaps most importantly, it has the power to transform classrooms into spaces where mistakes are not feared, but welcomed — not as failures, but as valuable data pointing the way forward. For me, to assess well is to teach well, and to teach well is to honor every dream that brought me here.</p>
          <p>This portfolio reflects that journey — honest, evolving, and deeply personal.</p>
        </div>
        <h3 class="goals-heading">Learning Goals at the Start of the Course</h3>
        <ul class="goals-list">
          <li><span class="goal-dot"></span><span>Understand the different types and purposes of assessment and how each serves a distinct function in teaching and learning.</span></li>
          <li><span class="goal-dot"></span><span>Learn how to design assessments that are fair, valid, and aligned with learning objectives.</span></li>
          <li><span class="goal-dot"></span><span>Develop the ability to interpret assessment data to guide instructional decisions and provide meaningful feedback.</span></li>
          <li><span class="goal-dot"></span><span>Build a personal philosophy of assessment rooted in both theory and lived experience.</span></li>
          <li><span class="goal-dot"></span><span>Gain confidence in using rubrics, test construction principles, and formative strategies in an actual classroom.</span></li>
        </ul>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>

  <!-- SECTION 02 -->
  <div id="s02">
    <div class="band">
      <div class="band-num">02</div>
      <div class="band-body">
        <p class="band-label">Section Two</p>
        <h2 class="band-title">Learning Artifacts &amp; Reflections</h2>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div style="background:var(--warm-white)">
      <div class="section-wrap">
        <p class="prose" style="font-style:italic;color:var(--muted);margin-bottom:3rem;">Four key topics from DPE 104, each presented with a full summary, sample output, personal reflection, and mastery explanation.</p>

        <!-- ── ARTIFACT 01 ── -->
        <div class="artifact-header" id="a01">
          <div class="artifact-num-badge">ARTIFACT 01</div>
          <div class="artifact-topic-title">Types &amp; Purposes of Assessment</div>
        </div>

        <h3 class="sub-heading">A. What I Learned</h3>
        <div class="prose">
          <p>This topic opened my eyes to the full landscape of assessment. I learned that assessment is not a single, monolithic event — it is a system built on three distinct types, each serving a specific role in the learning cycle. Understanding these types fundamentally changed how I see instruction itself.</p>
        </div>

        <p class="table-label">The Three Types of Assessment</p>
        <div class="compare-grid">
          <div class="compare-card">
            <div class="compare-card-title">Diagnostic Assessment</div>
            <div class="compare-row"><strong>Purpose</strong>Reveals what students already know before instruction begins</div>
            <div class="compare-row"><strong>Timing</strong>Before the start of a unit or lesson</div>
            <div class="compare-row"><strong>Stakes</strong>No grade — purely informational</div>
            <div class="compare-row"><strong>Examples</strong>KWL charts, pre-tests, entrance tickets, concept maps</div>
            <div class="compare-row"><strong>Key Question</strong>Where are my students right now?</div>
          </div>
          <div class="compare-card">
            <div class="compare-card-title">Formative vs. Summative</div>
            <div class="compare-row"><strong>Formative</strong>During learning — adjusts instruction in real time (low-stakes)</div>
            <div class="compare-row"><strong>Summative</strong>After learning — evaluates mastery at the end (high-stakes)</div>
            <div class="compare-row"><strong>Key Insight</strong>Both are essential; neither alone is sufficient. Formative without summative = no accountability checkpoint. Summative without formative = students arrive unprepared.</div>
          </div>
        </div>

        <p class="table-label">The Three Functions of Assessment</p>
        <table class="styled-table">
          <thead><tr><th>Function</th><th>Meaning</th><th>Who Benefits</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><td>Assessment FOR Learning</td><td>Provides ongoing feedback to improve learning while it is happening</td><td>Student &amp; Teacher</td></tr>
            <tr><td>Assessment AS Learning</td><td>Student becomes the assessor — self-monitoring and metacognition</td><td>Student (primary)</td></tr>
            <tr><td>Assessment OF Learning</td><td>Measures and reports what has been learned at the end of instruction</td><td>Teacher, Admin, Parents</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>

        <div class="prose">
          <p>I also learned the importance of alignment — diagnostic, formative, and summative assessments must all connect to the same learning objectives. When they are disconnected, students receive contradictory signals about what matters, and the data the teacher collects loses its meaning.</p>
        </div>

        <h3 class="sub-heading">B. Sample Output</h3>
        <div class="artifact-box">
          <p class="artifact-label">Artifact · The Assessment Cycle — Concept Map</p>
          <p>I designed a concept map that visually illustrated how all three assessment types connect within the instructional cycle. The map showed how diagnostic data shapes lesson planning, formative feedback adjusts instruction mid-stream, and summative results inform the design of the next unit. Arrows moved in a loop — emphasizing that assessment is never linear, but circular and ongoing. The map also distinguished the three functions (for/as/of learning), placing each at its appropriate point in the cycle with concrete classroom examples for each type.</p>
        </div>

        <div class="artifact-image-wrap">
          <img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="The Assessment Cycle — Concept Map" class="artifact-img" />
          <p class="artifact-img-caption">Figure 1 · The Assessment Cycle — Concept Map</p>
        </div>

        <h3 class="sub-heading">C. Personal Reflection</h3>
        <div class="reflection-block">
          <p class="reflection-label">How This Improved My Understanding</p>
          <p>Before this topic, I thought of assessment as something that happened after teaching — a final check to see who had paid attention. I now understand it as a continuous, purposeful system that operates before, during, and after instruction. The distinction between diagnostic, formative, and summative types gave me a framework I did not have before — one that makes me a more intentional planner.</p>
          <p>Most significantly, I realized that skipping diagnostic assessment means I begin teaching without evidence. I am making assumptions about my students rather than responding to who they actually are. That gap between assumption and reality is where so much classroom inequity lives.</p>
        </div>
        <div class="reflection-block">
          <p class="reflection-label">How I Would Apply This in an Actual Classroom</p>
          <p>I will begin every unit with a diagnostic activity — even something as simple as a 3-question pre-test or an entrance slip asking students to write what they already know. The results will not be graded. They will shape my planning. I will not teach what students already know, and I will not skip what they do not.</p>
          <p>I will also make assessment functions visible to my students. At the start of the year, I will explain: some assessments are for you — to help you grow; some are by you — to help you think about your own learning; and some are of you — to report your progress. When students understand why an assessment exists, they engage with it differently.</p>
        </div>
        <div class="reflection-block">
          <p class="reflection-label">E. Demonstrated Mastery</p>
          <p>This artifact demonstrates my understanding that assessment is purposeful, cyclical, and multifunctional. I can identify the role of each assessment type, explain their alignment to instruction, and describe how to apply all three appropriately within a real secondary classroom.</p>
        </div>

        <div class="artifact-divider"></div>

        <!-- ── ARTIFACT 02 ── -->
        <div class="artifact-header" id="a02">
          <div class="artifact-num-badge">ARTIFACT 02</div>
          <div class="artifact-topic-title">Principles of High-Quality Assessment</div>
        </div>

        <h3 class="sub-heading">A. What I Learned</h3>
        <div class="prose">
          <p>This topic gave me the vocabulary and criteria to evaluate the quality of any assessment — not just design one. I learned that assessment quality rests on four foundational principles, and that all four must be present simultaneously. A test that is valid but unfair, or reliable but impractical, fails as a classroom tool.</p>
        </div>

        <p class="table-label">The Four Principles of Assessment Quality</p>
        <table class="styled-table">
          <thead><tr><th>Principle</th><th>What It Means</th><th>Classroom Implication</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><td>Validity</td><td>The assessment measures exactly what it claims to measure — no more, no less.</td><td>If the objective is to evaluate writing skills, do not grade for neatness or spelling unless those are stated objectives.</td></tr>
            <tr><td>Reliability</td><td>The assessment produces consistent results across different students, times, and scorers.</td><td>Use clear rubrics and standardized conditions so the same work receives the same score regardless of who grades it.</td></tr>
            <tr><td>Fairness</td><td>All students have an equitable opportunity to demonstrate their learning.</td><td>Avoid cultural biases, ambiguous language, and format assumptions that disadvantage certain groups of students.</td></tr>
            <tr><td>Practicality</td><td>The assessment is feasible given available time, resources, and classroom context.</td><td>A 3-hour performance task for a 45-minute period is theoretically valid but practically useless. Design within real constraints.</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>

        <div class="prose">
          <p>I also learned that beyond these four principles, every assessment must sit within an alignment triangle: Learning Objective → Instruction → Assessment. When any one corner is misaligned, the entire triangle collapses. For example, if I teach critical thinking but assess only memorization, my summative data reflects what I tested — not what I taught. This misalignment produces invalid results, unfair comparisons, and meaningless grades.</p>
        </div>

        <h3 class="sub-heading">B. Sample Output</h3>
        <div class="artifact-box">
          <p class="artifact-label">Artifact · Assessment Quality Evaluation Checklist</p>
          <p>I designed a pre-administration checklist that I can use before giving any classroom assessment. The checklist includes criteria grouped under each quality principle:</p>
          <p style="margin-top:0.8rem;"><strong style="color:var(--gold-light);">Validity:</strong> Does every item directly target a stated learning objective? Is there any item that tests something not taught?</p>
          <p><strong style="color:var(--gold-light);">Reliability:</strong> Are the instructions clear and unambiguous? Is the rubric specific enough that two different teachers would score it the same way?</p>
          <p><strong style="color:var(--gold-light);">Fairness:</strong> Does any item assume cultural or linguistic knowledge not all students possess? Could a student with a disability access this task without unfair disadvantage?</p>
          <p><strong style="color:var(--gold-light);">Practicality:</strong> Can this assessment be administered within the available time? Can I score it within a reasonable turnaround period?</p>
        </div>

        <div class="artifact-image-wrap">
          <img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Assessment Quality Evaluation Checklist" class="artifact-img" />
          <p class="artifact-img-caption">Figure 2 · Assessment Quality Evaluation Checklist</p>
        </div>

        <h3 class="sub-heading">C. Personal Reflection</h3>
        <div class="reflection-block">
          <p class="reflection-label">How This Improved My Understanding</p>
          <p>The principle that affected me most deeply was fairness. I had always thought of assessment quality in technical terms — does it measure what it claims to? But this topic revealed that a test can be technically valid and still be deeply unjust. A question that uses idiomatic language, references a cultural practice, or assumes a particular home background immediately disadvantages students whose lived experiences differ from the assessor's default. That is not a measurement problem. That is an equity problem.</p>
          <p>Learning about the alignment triangle also sharpened my understanding of validity in a practical sense. I had designed assessments before without ever asking: does this actually match what I taught? This topic made that question unavoidable.</p>
        </div>
        <div class="reflection-block">
          <p class="reflection-label">How I Would Apply This in an Actual Classroom</p>
          <p>Before administering any major assessment, I will run it through my checklist — every time. I will also ask a colleague to review it for language bias or fairness issues, because some biases are invisible to the person who wrote the test. A fresh pair of eyes is a fairness tool.</p>
          <p>For alignment, I will begin every unit by writing the assessment before planning the lessons — using backward design. This ensures my instruction stays pointed at what students will actually be asked to demonstrate. If I design the test first, I cannot accidentally teach toward something else.</p>
        </div>
        <div class="reflection-block">
          <p class="reflection-label">E. Demonstrated Mastery</p>
          <p>This artifact demonstrates my ability to evaluate assessments using established quality criteria. I understand that valid, reliable, fair, and practical assessments are not accidents — they are the result of deliberate, principle-driven design that protects every student's right to be assessed equitably.</p>
        </div>

        <div class="artifact-divider"></div>

        <!-- ── ARTIFACT 03 ── -->
        <div class="artifact-header" id="a03">
          <div class="artifact-num-badge">ARTIFACT 03</div>
          <div class="artifact-topic-title">Rubrics, Test Construction, and Validity</div>
        </div>

        <h3 class="sub-heading">A. What I Learned</h3>
        <div class="prose">
          <p>This was the most hands-on and technically demanding topic in the course — and the most immediately applicable. I learned how to build assessments from scratch, guided by principles rather than habit. I stopped copying test formats I had seen before and started asking: what does validity actually require here?</p>
        </div>

        <p class="table-label">Test Construction Principles</p>
        <table class="styled-table">
          <thead><tr><th>Principle</th><th>What It Means in Practice</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><td>Table of Specifications</td><td>Maps test items to specific learning objectives and cognitive levels (e.g., Bloom's Taxonomy). Ensures the test is proportionally balanced — no objective is over- or under-represented.</td></tr>
            <tr><td>Item Clarity</td><td>Every test item should have exactly one defensible correct answer (for objective items) or clear, observable criteria (for performance tasks). Ambiguity is the enemy of reliability.</td></tr>
            <tr><td>Item Difficulty Balance</td><td>A well-constructed test includes items across difficulty levels — not all easy, not all hard. This allows the test to discriminate between students at different levels of mastery.</td></tr>
            <tr><td>Alignment to Instruction</td><td>Only test what was taught. An item testing content never covered in class is not rigorous — it is unfair, and it produces invalid data about student learning.</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>

        <p class="table-label" style="margin-top:2rem;">Holistic vs. Analytic Rubrics</p>
        <div class="compare-grid">
          <div class="compare-card">
            <div class="compare-card-title">Holistic Rubric</div>
            <div class="compare-row"><strong>Scoring</strong>Single overall score for the entire performance</div>
            <div class="compare-row"><strong>Best for</strong>Quick assessments, portfolio scoring, or holistic impression</div>
            <div class="compare-row"><strong>Advantage</strong>Fast to score</div>
            <div class="compare-row"><strong>Disadvantage</strong>Students receive minimal feedback on what to improve</div>
            <div class="compare-row"><strong>Example</strong>A 4-point scale assessing a speech as a whole</div>
          </div>
          <div class="compare-card">
            <div class="compare-card-title">Analytic Rubric</div>
            <div class="compare-row"><strong>Scoring</strong>Separate scores per criterion — each scored independently</div>
            <div class="compare-row"><strong>Best for</strong>Complex tasks where specific feedback is needed</div>
            <div class="compare-row"><strong>Advantage</strong>Highly actionable — students know exactly where to improve</div>
            <div class="compare-row"><strong>Disadvantage</strong>Takes longer to score</div>
            <div class="compare-row"><strong>Example</strong>Scoring a speech on Content, Delivery, Organization, and Language separately</div>
          </div>
        </div>

        <h3 class="sub-heading">B. Sample Output</h3>
        <div class="artifact-box">
          <p class="artifact-label">Artifact · Original 4-Point Analytic Rubric — Secondary Science Oral Recitation</p>
          <p>I designed an analytic rubric for a secondary Science oral recitation task with five criteria, each rated on a 4-point scale (Beginning, Developing, Proficient, Advanced). Each performance level was defined with specific, observable behavioral descriptors — not vague adjectives.</p>
        </div>
        <table class="styled-table">
          <thead><tr><th>Criterion</th><th>Beginning (1)</th><th>Developing (2)</th><th>Proficient (3)</th><th>Advanced (4)</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><td>Content Accuracy</td><td>Major factual errors; concepts missing</td><td>Some errors; key concepts partially present</td><td>Mostly accurate; minor gaps</td><td>Fully accurate; rich conceptual depth</td></tr>
            <tr><td>Clarity of Explanation</td><td>Explanation unclear; hard to follow</td><td>Somewhat clear; some confusing parts</td><td>Generally clear and logical</td><td>Exceptionally clear; easy to follow</td></tr>
            <tr><td>Scientific Terminology</td><td>No scientific terms used</td><td>1–2 terms used, often incorrectly</td><td>Several terms used correctly</td><td>Precise use of terms throughout</td></tr>
            <tr><td>Organization</td><td>No discernible structure</td><td>Some structure; hard to follow</td><td>Clear intro, body, conclusion</td><td>Seamless, polished structure</td></tr>
            <tr><td>Confidence &amp; Delivery</td><td>Reads from notes; no eye contact</td><td>Occasional eye contact; hesitant</td><td>Confident; mostly without notes</td><td>Commanding; fully natural delivery</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>

        <h3 class="sub-heading">C. Personal Reflection</h3>
        <div class="reflection-block">
          <p class="reflection-label">How This Improved My Understanding</p>
          <p>Building a rubric from scratch was humbling. It forced me to answer a question I had never taken seriously: what does excellent actually look like — specifically, observably, in this particular task? I discovered that vague descriptors like 'good' or 'needs improvement' are useless to students. They do not tell a learner where they are or what to do next. Observable, behavioral descriptions do both.</p>
          <p>The Table of Specifications exercise also revealed a gap in how I thought about test design. I had always assumed a test was balanced — until I mapped it and found that 80% of my items were at the lowest cognitive level. That was not a test of learning. It was a test of memorization.</p>
        </div>
        <div class="reflection-block">
          <p class="reflection-label">How I Would Apply This in an Actual Classroom</p>
          <p>I will always share the rubric with students before the task begins — not after it is graded. A rubric shared at the start is a teaching tool. A rubric revealed only at grading time is a surprise. I refuse to surprise my students with expectations.</p>
          <p>I will use analytic rubrics for all major performance tasks, specifically because they tell students where to improve — not just how much they missed. And I will use a TOS every time I write a unit test, to make sure my items are proportionally aligned to what I actually spent time teaching. These are not extra steps. They are the steps that make assessment fair.</p>
        </div>
        <div class="reflection-block">
          <p class="reflection-label">E. Demonstrated Mastery</p>
          <p>This artifact demonstrates my technical competence in assessment construction. I can design valid test items using a TOS, build analytic rubrics with specific behavioral descriptors, and apply backward design principles to ensure alignment between what is taught, what is assessed, and what feedback is given.</p>
        </div>

        <div class="artifact-divider"></div>

        <!-- ── ARTIFACT 04 ── -->
        <div class="artifact-header" id="a04">
          <div class="artifact-num-badge">ARTIFACT 04</div>
          <div class="artifact-topic-title">Formative vs. Summative Assessment</div>
        </div>

        <h3 class="sub-heading">A. What I Learned</h3>
        <div class="prose">
          <p>This topic gave me the clearest and most practically useful distinction in the entire course. I learned that formative and summative assessments are not just different types — they are different philosophies of assessment, each with its own purpose, timing, stakes, and role in the learning relationship between teacher and student.</p>
        </div>

        <div class="compare-grid">
          <div class="compare-card">
            <div class="compare-card-title">Formative Assessment</div>
            <div class="compare-row"><strong>Purpose</strong>To improve learning while it is happening</div>
            <div class="compare-row"><strong>Timing</strong>During instruction — ongoing</div>
            <div class="compare-row"><strong>Stakes</strong>Low — ungraded or minimally graded</div>
            <div class="compare-row"><strong>Audience</strong>Teacher and student</div>
            <div class="compare-row"><strong>Examples</strong>Exit tickets, think-pair-share, whiteboards, KWL charts, peer review</div>
            <div class="compare-row"><strong>Key Question</strong>What does the student need next?</div>
          </div>
          <div class="compare-card">
            <div class="compare-card-title">Summative Assessment</div>
            <div class="compare-row"><strong>Purpose</strong>To measure learning after instruction ends</div>
            <div class="compare-row"><strong>Timing</strong>End of unit, quarter, or semester</div>
            <div class="compare-row"><strong>Stakes</strong>High — contributes to final grade</div>
            <div class="compare-row"><strong>Audience</strong>Teacher, parents, administration</div>
            <div class="compare-row"><strong>Examples</strong>Final exams, standardized tests, term papers, performance tasks</div>
            <div class="compare-row"><strong>Key Question</strong>Did the student meet the standard?</div>
          </div>
        </div>

        <p class="table-label" style="margin-top:2rem;">Side-by-Side Comparison</p>
        <table class="styled-table">
          <thead><tr><th>Aspect</th><th>Formative</th><th>Summative</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><td>Purpose</td><td>Improve learning in progress</td><td>Certify learning at the end</td></tr>
            <tr><td>Timing</td><td>During instruction</td><td>After instruction</td></tr>
            <tr><td>Frequency</td><td>Frequent &amp; ongoing</td><td>Infrequent — end of term</td></tr>
            <tr><td>Feedback</td><td>Immediate &amp; specific</td><td>Delayed; often just a grade</td></tr>
            <tr><td>Stakes</td><td>Low — no grade penalty</td><td>High — affects final grade</td></tr>
            <tr><td>Use of Data</td><td>Adjust teaching &amp; pacing</td><td>Report, promote, certify</td></tr>
            <tr><td>Student Role</td><td>Active — self-monitors</td><td>Passive — demonstrates mastery</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>

        <h3 class="sub-heading">B. Sample Output</h3>
        <div class="artifact-box">
          <p class="artifact-label">Artifact · Formative Assessment Strategy Toolkit — 10 Strategies for Secondary Classrooms</p>
          <p>I curated a personal toolkit of 10 formative assessment strategies, each evaluated for time required, data generated, and best-fit subject area.</p>
        </div>
        <div class="strategies-grid">
          <div class="strategy-card"><div class="strat-num">01</div><div class="strat-name">Exit Ticket</div><div class="strat-desc">Students answer 1–2 questions at the end of class. Teacher reviews overnight to plan the next lesson based on actual evidence, not assumption.</div></div>
          <div class="strategy-card"><div class="strat-num">02</div><div class="strat-name">Think-Pair-Share</div><div class="strat-desc">Students think individually, discuss with a partner, then share with the class. Surfaces misconceptions in real time and promotes accountable talk.</div></div>
          <div class="strategy-card"><div class="strat-num">03</div><div class="strat-name">Traffic Light</div><div class="strat-desc">Students self-rate understanding: Red (lost), Yellow (unsure), Green (confident). Builds metacognition and tells the teacher who needs support immediately.</div></div>
          <div class="strategy-card"><div class="strat-num">04</div><div class="strat-name">Muddiest Point</div><div class="strat-desc">Students write the one thing still unclear. Teacher uses responses to open the next class with targeted clarification — before moving forward.</div></div>
          <div class="strategy-card"><div class="strat-num">05</div><div class="strat-name">Mini Whiteboard</div><div class="strat-desc">Students write answers simultaneously and hold up boards. Teacher gets an instant whole-class snapshot of understanding without individual pressure.</div></div>
          <div class="strategy-card"><div class="strat-num">06</div><div class="strat-name">One-Minute Paper</div><div class="strat-desc">Students write for 60 seconds: most important thing learned + one remaining question. Excellent for content-heavy lessons.</div></div>
          <div class="strategy-card"><div class="strat-num">07</div><div class="strat-name">Gallery Walk</div><div class="strat-desc">Students rotate around posted work or prompts, adding comments. Encourages peer learning and gives teacher data on reasoning and critical thinking.</div></div>
          <div class="strategy-card"><div class="strat-num">08</div><div class="strat-name">Peer Feedback</div><div class="strat-desc">Students review each other's work using structured starters: 'I noticed...', 'I wonder if...', 'One strength is...'. Develops evaluation skills.</div></div>
          <div class="strategy-card"><div class="strat-num">09</div><div class="strat-name">Digital Poll / Kahoot</div><div class="strat-desc">Quick tech-based polling reveals class-wide understanding patterns instantly. Results projected and discussed — turns data into a learning moment.</div></div>
          <div class="strategy-card"><div class="strat-num">10</div><div class="strat-name">Observational Checklist</div><div class="strat-desc">Teacher circulates during tasks, marking skill indicators on a prepared checklist. Captures real performance evidence without formal testing pressure.</div></div>
        </div>

        <h3 class="sub-heading">C. Personal Reflection</h3>
        <div class="reflection-block">
          <p class="reflection-label">How This Improved My Understanding</p>
          <p>This topic resolved a tension I had carried without words. I had always felt that final exams did not fully capture what my students were capable of — but I could not explain why, and I did not know what to do instead. Now I can. Summative assessments, by design, produce delayed, low-specificity data that students cannot act on. Formative assessment fills the gap — in real time, with feedback that has somewhere to go.</p>
          <p>I also came to understand something that surprised me: a student who is shocked by their final exam grade is evidence that they did not receive enough honest formative feedback. The failure belongs as much to the process as it does to the student. That realization made me feel responsible in a new way.</p>
        </div>
        <div class="reflection-block">
          <p class="reflection-label">How I Would Apply This in an Actual Classroom</p>
          <p>I will end every single lesson with a formative check — even a one-question exit ticket. Not to grade. To listen. To enter the next class with data, not assumptions. I will also use summative results not as final verdicts, but as mirrors: what did my students learn, and what did my teaching miss? Both questions matter equally.</p>
          <p>I will teach my students the difference between formative and summative assessments at the start of the year — in plain language. When students understand why an exit ticket exists (to help them, not grade them), they participate honestly. That honesty is the data I need to teach well.</p>
        </div>
        <div class="reflection-block">
          <p class="reflection-label">E. Demonstrated Mastery</p>
          <p>This artifact demonstrates a strong command of both assessment types — their purposes, timing, and complementary roles. I can design formative strategies for real secondary classrooms, read summative data critically, and articulate a philosophy that places student growth at the center of every assessment decision.</p>
        </div>

      </div>
    </div>
  </div>

  <!-- SECTION 03 -->
  <div id="s03">
    <div class="band">
      <div class="band-num">03</div>
      <div class="band-body">
        <p class="band-label">Section Three</p>
        <h2 class="band-title">My Assessment Philosophy</h2>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div style="background:var(--cream)">
      <div class="section-wrap">
        <div class="prose">
          <p>I used to believe that assessment was something a teacher did to students. You taught. They listened. You tested. They answered. A number appeared, and that number — I believed — told the truth. It told you who was smart, who was struggling, who deserved to move on. I carried that belief quietly and without question, the way you carry assumptions you have never had a reason to examine.</p>
          <p>Then this course made me examine it. And what I found underneath that belief shook me.</p>
        </div>

        <div class="philosophy-quote">
          "A grade is not a truth. It is a snapshot —<br>
          and snapshots can lie if taken at the wrong moment,<br>
          in the wrong light, without enough context."
        </div>

        <div class="prose">
          <p>I have learned — not merely intellectually, but in a sense that has become a part of who I am — that assessment is relational work. In each instance when the teacher creates an activity, provides a comment on the piece of writing done by a learner, takes a break during the lesson and asks a question while listening to its answer, a teacher says something about his or her perception of a certain potential inherent in the student. Assessment is never impartial; rather, it is a picture drawn of the way a teacher views a particular learner.</p>
          <p>Before this course, my views on assessments were quite black-and-white, with a clear distinction between quizzes and exams. I knew terms such as "formative" and "summative," but they meant nothing to me. Today, however, there appear to be two entirely separate theories residing in one room together. Formative assessments are an ongoing and low-stakes dialogue between a student and a teacher, the kind that says, "I know your current level of competence, and here is how you will get better." This is the purpose behind formative assessments — they are done for the benefit of the learner, rather than to grade. Summative assessments are the culminating event, marking the conclusion of the learning period — and I strongly believe that, ideally, there should be no surprises here. If a student is surprised by a bad score on a final test, it means they were not provided with adequate formative assessments.</p>
        </div>

        <div class="philosophy-quote">
          "The most powerful thing a teacher can offer a student<br>
          is not a grade. It is a mirror —<br>
          clear, specific, and kind enough<br>
          to show them exactly where to go next."
        </div>

        <div class="prose">
          <p>This shift in understanding has given shape to the teacher I intend to become. I will share rubrics with students before a task begins — not after. Because a student who does not know what is being asked of them is not being assessed; they are being ambushed, and I refuse to ambush my students. I will close every lesson with a formative check: an exit ticket, a whiteboard response, a quiet minute to write down the one thing still unclear. Not to grade — but to listen. The most dangerous assumption in teaching is walking out of a class believing "they got it" without a single piece of evidence that they did. I will not make that assumption. I will look for the evidence, every single day.</p>
          <p>In feedback, I will write to the students, not just about the work. Not "unclear argument" but "Your idea has something real to say. Let it say it louder." Feedback that sees the person behind the paper, that names both the strength and the gap, and that always — always — points toward what is possible.</p>
          <p>In remediation, I will hold on to the belief that failure is not a conclusion. When a student does not meet a standard, my first question will not be "What grade do I give?" but "What did they need that I have not yet provided?" That question keeps me honest. It keeps me from making the classroom about my performance and reminds me it has always been about theirs.</p>
          <p>In grading, I will measure only what I taught, and only what I taught. Grades will not carry the weight of a student's personality, participation habits, or the kind of week they were having. A grade must mean something clean and clear: here is the evidence of what you learned. Nothing more, and nothing less.</p>
        </div>

        <div class="philosophy-quote">
          "I want to be the kind of teacher whose students<br>
          walk out of a unit not asking, 'What did I get?'<br>
          but 'What did I learn?'"
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>

<script>
  function openPortfolio() {
    const cover = document.getElementById('cover');
    const portfolio = document.getElementById('portfolio');
    cover.classList.add('hidden');
    setTimeout(() => {
      cover.style.display = 'none';
      portfolio.classList.add('visible');
      window.scrollTo(0,0);
    }, 800);
  }

  const sections = ['s01','s02','s03','s04'];
  const navLinks = document.querySelectorAll('.nav-links a');
  window.addEventListener('scroll', () => {
    let current = '';
    sections.forEach(id => {
      const el = document.getElementById(id);
      if (el && window.scrollY >= el.offsetTop - 80) current = id;
    });
    navLinks.forEach(a => {
      a.classList.toggle('active', a.getAttribute('href') === '#' + current);
    });
  });
</script>
